lessons.title: Planning the climb and checking the tree
lessons.html:
Planning the climb

Tree work in parks, gardens, farms and estates often needs someone to climb: to prune branches, remove dead wood, fit cables or inspect for pests. Falls from trees cause serious injuries and deaths. This unit gives the basic principles. You may only climb after hands-on training and under the supervision of a qualified arborist, using equipment your employer has issued and checked.

Check the site

  • Power lines: look up. If any branch is near overhead lines, stop. Only authorised, specially trained people may work near live lines, and the power supplier may need to switch off. Electricity can jump through branches and ropes.
  • Weather: never climb in strong wind, rain, lightning or when branches are wet and slippery.
  • Drop zone: mark off the area under the tree with cones and tape. Keep people, vehicles and animals out.
  • Obstacles: roofs, fences, glasshouses and paving that falling branches could damage.

Check the tree

Walk around the tree and look from the roots to the top:

  • Dead branches, hanging broken branches (hangers).
  • Cracks, splits and cavities in the trunk.
  • Fungus (mushrooms or brackets) on the trunk or roots, a sign of rot.
  • Lifting soil or broken roots, signs the tree could fall.
  • Bees, wasps, snakes or birds' nests.
  • Thorns or irritating sap.

If the tree looks unsafe to climb, do not climb. Report it. It may need a cherry picker (aerial platform) or a different method.

Plan with the team

  • Agree on the job: which branches, in what order.
  • Choose the anchor point: a strong, live branch high in the tree for the climbing rope.
  • A trained ground worker must always be present. Never climb alone.
  • Agree on signals or use radios.
  • Have a rescue plan: who will rescue the climber if they are hurt in the tree, and how.

lessons.title: Equipment and safe climbing
lessons.html:
Equipment

Personal protective equipment

  • Helmet with chin strap, made for tree work or climbing.
  • Eye protection against sawdust and twigs.
  • Hearing protection when saws are used.
  • Gloves and sturdy boots with good grip.
  • Chainsaw trousers if a chainsaw is used (only by certified operators).

Climbing equipment

  • Climbing harness.
  • Climbing rope made for tree climbing.
  • Lanyard (a short adjustable rope) for a second attachment.
  • Karabiners (locking connectors) that lock automatically.
  • Throw line and throw bag to set the rope.

Inspect before every climb

Check ropes for cuts, burns, fluff or stiff spots. Check harness stitching and buckles. Check karabiners open, close and lock properly. Damaged equipment must be taken out of service and reported. Never use a rope that has been cut, burnt or held a heavy fall.

Safe climbing principles

  1. Always be tied in. From the moment you leave the ground until you are back on the ground, you are attached to the tree by rope.
  2. Two attachments when cutting. Use your climbing rope and your lanyard when you use a saw, so one cut cannot drop you.
  3. Three points of contact when moving: two hands and a foot, or two feet and a hand.
  4. Test branches before putting weight on them. Stay close to the trunk on thin branches.
  5. Check karabiners are locked every time you clip in. Your partner on the ground checks too before you start.
  6. Keep tools tied to your harness so they do not fall.
  7. Shout a warning before dropping branches. Wait for the ground worker to say all clear.
  8. Never cut your own rope. Know where it is at all times.

Coming down

Descend slowly and in control. Clear tools and branches from the drop zone. Inspect and pack equipment, and record any damage.

Key points

  • Climb only after hands-on training, with a ground worker and a rescue plan.
  • Check for power lines, weather and tree defects before climbing.
  • Mark off the drop zone.
  • Inspect all equipment before every climb.
  • Always be tied in, and use two attachments when cutting.
